clinicalPearls: The generalised, sclerodermoid form of lichen myxoedematosus, characterised by widespread firm waxy papules, dermal mucin deposition, fibroblast proliferation and an associated monoclonal gammopathy
Numerous closely set, dome-shaped papules are typically arranged in a linear array over the face, ears, neck, trunk and hands, with progressive skin thickening and induration

Characteristic signs include the doughnut sign (a central depression surrounded by a raised rim over the proximal interphalangeal joints), deep glabellar furrows producing leonine facies, and reduced mouth opening
A monoclonal paraprotein, most often IgG with lambda light chains, is present in the large majority, although progression to overt myeloma is uncommon
Systemic involvement may affect the gastrointestinal tract (dysphagia, dysmotility), muscles (proximal myopathy), heart, kidneys and nervous system
The dermato-neuro syndrome, an abrupt encephalopathy with fever, seizures and coma, is a rare but life-threatening complication requiring emergency treatment

Intravenous immunoglobulin is generally first-line therapy, with options such as thalidomide or lenalidomide, systemic corticosteroids, bortezomib and autologous stem-cell transplantation for refractory or systemic disease
reference.pathophysiology: Scleromyxoedema is a primary cutaneous mucinosis in which fibroblasts, apparently stimulated by circulating factors, proliferate and deposit excess glycosaminoglycans (chiefly hyaluronic acid) together with increased collagen in the upper and mid dermis. A monoclonal gammopathy is almost always present, and the paraprotein or associated cytokines are thought to drive fibroblast activation and mucin production, though the precise mechanism linking the two is not fully understood. The resulting combination of dermal mucin, fibroblast proliferation and fibrosis accounts for the papular and sclerodermoid skin changes, while similar processes in other organs underlie the systemic and neurological complications.
additionalDifferentials: Localised forms of lichen myxoedematosus without paraproteinaemia
Scleromyxoedema-like changes of the reticular erythematous mucinosis or lupus spectrum
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy showing dermal mucin deposition, fibroblast proliferation and fibrosis
Serum protein electrophoresis and immunofixation to detect and characterise the paraprotein
Serum free light chains and quantitative immunoglobulins
Bone marrow examination to assess for a plasma cell dyscrasia
Colloidal iron or Alcian blue staining of biopsy to confirm mucin
Screening for systemic involvement with cardiac, oesophageal, muscle and renal assessment as indicated
Neuroimaging and lumbar puncture if dermato-neuro syndrome is suspected
redFlags: Abrupt fever, confusion, seizures or coma indicating dermato-neuro syndrome
Progressive dysphagia or aspiration from oesophageal dysmotility
Cardiac or renal involvement suggesting extensive systemic disease
Evidence of transformation to multiple myeloma
Severe proximal weakness compromising mobility or respiration
reference.prognosis: Scleromyxoedema is a chronic, unpredictable and potentially progressive disorder that can be complicated by fatal systemic and neurological involvement. Response to intravenous immunoglobulin and other therapies has improved outcomes, but relapses are common and the dermato-neuro syndrome carries a high mortality.
pitfalls: Failing to search for and monitor the associated monoclonal gammopathy
Mistaking the condition for systemic sclerosis and missing the distinctive papular and doughnut-sign features
Not recognising dermato-neuro syndrome, a treatable but rapidly fatal emergency, as part of the disease
Overlooking systemic organ involvement while focusing on the skin
Assuming a normal bone marrow excludes significant paraprotein-related disease
management: Give intravenous immunoglobulin as the treatment of choice for the cutaneous and systemic manifestations
Escalate to plasma-cell-directed therapy such as systemic corticosteroids, thalidomide or lenalidomide, or bortezomib with autologous stem-cell transplantation in resistant cases
Manage the dermato-neuro syndrome of encephalopathy, seizures, and coma as a life-threatening emergency with intravenous immunoglobulin, corticosteroids, and plasma exchange
Provide supportive care for dysphagia and dysmotility, proximal myopathy, and reduced mouth opening
Monitor for gastrointestinal, muscular, cardiac, renal, and neurological involvement
Refer to haematology to characterise the IgG-lambda paraprotein and exclude progression to myeloma
Coordinate multidisciplinary dermatology, haematology, and neurology follow-up given the relapsing, unpredictable course
